cse-2026-2-cs-17.approach: Integrate term by term over the symmetric interval $[-1,1]$: the odd term $-ax$ integrates to $0$, so $I(a)$ is a constant. Then read each statement against that constant.
concepts: Odd and even functions on a symmetric interval

steps.title: Add them
steps.body:
$$I(a) = 2 - a\cdot 0 + 2 = 4 \quad\text{for every real } a.$$
So $I(a)$ does not depend on $a$ (A true, B false), $I(a) = 4 > 0$ for every $a$ (C true), and it is never negative (D false).

optionAnalysis.reason: The $a$-term is $-a\int_{-1}^{1}x\,dx = -a\cdot 0 = 0$, so $I(a) = 4$ whatever $a$ is.
Would need $\int_{-1}^{1} x\,dx \ne 0$; but $x$ is odd on a symmetric interval, so its integral is $0$.
$I(a) = 4 > 0$ for every $a$, so certainly some $a$ (e.g. $a = 0$) gives a positive value.
$I(a)$ is always $4$, never negative. Choosing a large $a$ does not help because the $a$-term vanishes.

cse-2026-2-cs-17.shortcut: On $[-1,1]$ odd terms vanish: keep only the even part $3x^2 + 1$, whose integral is $2\int_0^1(3x^2+1)\,dx = 2(1+1) = 4$.
pitfalls: Thinking a parameter in the integrand must make the value vary with it — here it multiplies an odd function.
Integrating $3x^2$ as $x^2$ or forgetting the factor from both halves of the interval.
cse-2026-2-cs-17.verification: Direct antiderivative: $F(x) = x^3 - \tfrac{a}{2}x^2 + x$; $F(1) - F(-1) = \left(2 - \tfrac a2\right) - \left(-2 - \tfrac a2\right) = 4$.

cse-2026-2-cs-18.approach: Convert the four 4-bit patterns to decimals; 4-bit two's complement holds only $[-8, 7]$, so an operation overflows exactly when its true result leaves that range (equivalently, two same-sign operands give a result of the other sign).

steps.title: A: N1 + N2
steps.body: $-5 + (-3) = -8$, inside the range. Bitwise: $1011 + 1101 = 1\,1000$, keep $1000 = -8$ (negative + negative = negative). **No overflow.**

steps.title: B: N2 + N3
steps.body: $-3 + (-6) = -9 < -8$. Bitwise: $1101 + 1010 = 1\,0111$, keep $0111 = +7$: two negatives gave a positive. **Overflow.**

steps.title: C: N3 − N4
steps.body: $-6 - (-7) = +1$, inside the range. Hardware adds the negation: $-N_4 = 0111$, and $1010 + 0111 = 1\,0001$, keep $0001 = 1$. Operands of opposite sign can never overflow. **No overflow.**

steps.title: D: N1 + N4
steps.body: $-5 + (-7) = -12 < -8$. Bitwise: $1011 + 1001 = 1\,0100$, keep $0100 = +4$: two negatives gave a positive. **Overflow.**

answer.value: Overflow occurs for **$N_2 + N_3$ and $N_1 + N_4$** — options (B) and (D)

optionAnalysis.reason: $-5 + (-3) = -8$ is exactly the most negative 4-bit value ($1000$), so it fits. Treating $-8$ as out of range is the trap.
$-3 + (-6) = -9 < -8$; the 4-bit sum $0111 = +7$ has the wrong sign.
$-6 - (-7) = +1$; adding $1010 + 0111$ gives $0001$. The end carry out is discarded and is not an overflow.
$-5 + (-7) = -12 < -8$; the 4-bit sum $0100 = +4$ has the wrong sign.

cse-2026-2-cs-18.shortcut: All four numbers are negative. Sums of two negatives overflow when the magnitudes add to more than $8$: $5+3 = 8$ (fits), $3+6 = 9$ and $5+7 = 12$ (overflow). A difference of two negatives cannot overflow.
pitfalls: Calling a carry out of the MSB an overflow — in two's complement, overflow means the carry into the MSB differs from the carry out of it.
Forgetting that $-8$ is representable in 4 bits, so $N_1 + N_2$ is fine.
Reading the patterns as unsigned numbers.
cse-2026-2-cs-18.verification: Carry rule: for $N_2+N_3$ ($1101+1010$) the carry into bit 3 is $0$ and the carry out is $1$ — they differ, overflow. For $N_1+N_2$ ($1011+1101$) both carries are $1$ — no overflow.

cse-2026-2-cs-19.approach: A grammar is ambiguous if one string has two different parse trees (or leftmost derivations). Look for a short witness string in each grammar; for the others, argue that each step of the derivation is forced.

steps.title: A and D are unambiguous
steps.body:
- (A) $S \to aSb \mid \epsilon$: every sentence is $a^nb^n$, and the only derivation applies $S \to aSb$ exactly $n$ times then $S \to \epsilon$. Each step is forced, so exactly one parse tree.
- (D) $S \to aS \mid \epsilon$: generates $a^n$ by $n$ uses of $S \to aS$ then $S \to \epsilon$ — again a single forced chain.

steps.title: B is ambiguous
steps.body:
For $id + id * id$:

1. $E \Rightarrow E + E \Rightarrow id + E \Rightarrow id + E * E \Rightarrow id + id * id$ (the $*$ is below the $+$)
2. $E \Rightarrow E * E \Rightarrow E + E * E \Rightarrow id + E * E \Rightarrow id + id * id$ (the $+$ is below the $*$)

Two different leftmost derivations, two parse trees — the grammar fixes neither precedence nor associativity.

scene.title: (B) two trees for id + id * id

steps.title: C is ambiguous
steps.body:
For the one-symbol string $a$:

1. $S \Rightarrow aS \Rightarrow a$ (using $S \to \epsilon$)
2. $S \Rightarrow Sa \Rightarrow a$ (using $S \to \epsilon$)

The roots use different productions, so the parse trees differ. ($S \to aS \mid Sa$ lets the $a$'s be added from either side.)

optionAnalysis.reason: Every string $a^nb^n$ has exactly one derivation ($n$ times $S \to aSb$, then $S \to \epsilon$); no choice ever arises.
$id + id * id$ has two leftmost derivations (start with $E \to E+E$ or with $E \to E*E$).
The string $a$ has two parse trees: $S \to aS$ or $S \to Sa$ at the root, each finished by $S \to \epsilon$.
Right-linear: each $a^n$ is produced by the unique chain $S \to aS$ ($n$ times), $S \to \epsilon$.

cse-2026-2-cs-19.shortcut: A production with the nonterminal on **both** sides of a symbol, or two productions that can build the same string from opposite ends ($S \to aS \mid Sa$), is a red flag — try the shortest string first.
pitfalls: Thinking A is ambiguous because it is not regular — ambiguity and regularity are unrelated.
Missing C: the language is just $a^*$, but the grammar (not the language) is what is ambiguous.
cse-2026-2-cs-19.verification: Count parse trees for $a^2$ in C: root $aS$ or $Sa$, and the inner $S$ for $a$ again has 2 choices, giving more than one tree; in D, $a^2$ has only $S \Rightarrow aS \Rightarrow aaS \Rightarrow aa$.

cse-2026-2-cs-20.approach: Compute $k \bmod 9$ for each key and count how many keys land in each slot; with chaining, a slot's chain length is simply its count.

steps.title: Build the chains
steps.body:
Insert in the given order (append to the slot's chain):

- slot 1: 28 → 19 → 10
- slot 3: 12
- slot 5: 5
- slot 6: 15 → 33
- slot 8: 26 → 17
- slots 0, 2, 4, 7: empty

steps.title: Longest chain
steps.body: Lengths are $0,3,0,1,0,1,2,0,2$ (sum $= 9$ keys ✓). The longest chain is at slot 1 with **3** keys.

cse-2026-2-cs-20.shortcut: Only the multiset of residues matters: residues $5,1,1,6,8,6,3,8,1$ — the value $1$ appears three times, nothing appears more.
pitfalls: Using $k \bmod 10$ or the table size from habit instead of $9$.
Counting collisions (2 at slot 1) instead of chain length (3).
cse-2026-2-cs-20.verification: Total keys over all chains: $3+1+1+2+2 = 9$, matching the 9 inserted keys.

animation.title: Hash table, h(k) = k mod 9, chaining

cse-2026-2-cs-21.approach: A $2\times 2$ system has infinitely many solutions only when the coefficient determinant is $0$ **and** the equations are consistent (the two rows are proportional including the right-hand side). Solve for $a$ first, then $b$.

steps.title: Singular coefficient matrix
steps.body:
$$\det\begin{bmatrix} a & 1 \\ 16 & a \end{bmatrix} = a^2 - 16 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; a = 4 \text{ or } a = -4$$
If $a^2 \ne 16$ the solution is unique, so multiple solutions force $a = \pm 4$.

steps.title: Consistency fixes b
steps.body:
The two equations must be multiples of each other: $\dfrac{a}{16} = \dfrac{1}{a} = \dfrac{b}{24}$.

- $a = 4$: $\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{b}{24} \Rightarrow b = 6$. (Check: $4x + y = 6$ times $4$ gives $16x + 4y = 24$ ✓)
- $a = -4$: $-\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{b}{24} \Rightarrow b = -6$. (Check: $-4x + y = -6$ times $-4$ gives $16x - 4y = 24$ ✓)

steps.title: Product
steps.body: Either way $ab = 4 \times 6 = 24$ or $ab = (-4)\times(-6) = 24$. So $ab = \mathbf{24}$.

cse-2026-2-cs-21.shortcut: Multiply the first equation by $a$: $a^2x + ay = ab$. For it to coincide with $16x + ay = 24$ you need $a^2 = 16$ and $ab = 24$ — the product drops out directly.
pitfalls: Stopping at $\det = 0$: with the wrong $b$ the system is inconsistent (no solution).
Taking only $a = 4$ and worrying the answer is ambiguous — both roots give the same product.
cse-2026-2-cs-21.verification: With $a = 4, b = 6$: every point on $y = 6 - 4x$ satisfies both equations, e.g. $(0, 6)$: $16\cdot 0 + 4\cdot 6 = 24$ ✓ and $(1, 2)$: $16 + 8 = 24$ ✓.

cse-2026-2-cs-22.approach: A merge of sorted $L$ and $R$ is void exactly when $\max(L) \le \min(R)$, i.e. the last element of $L$ does not exceed the first of $R$. Walk the 7 merges of top-down merge sort and test that one comparison each time.

steps.title: Void test
steps.body: The merge outputs $L$ then $R$ unchanged iff every element of $L$ is $\le$ every element of $R$, i.e. $L_{\text{last}} \le R_{\text{first}}$ (both runs are sorted). The 7 merges are the 7 internal nodes of the recursion tree: 4 merges of singletons, 2 of pairs, 1 final.

steps.title: Final merge and count
steps.body:
$L = [7, 8, 10, 19]$, $R = [25, 31, 35, 41]$: $19 \le 25$, so the output is $L$ followed by $R$ — **void**.

Void merges: $[8]+[19]$, $[25]+[31]$ and the final merge, a total of $\mathbf{3}$.

cse-2026-2-cs-22.shortcut: Void at a node $\iff$ the left half's maximum $\le$ the right half's minimum. Left/right maxima-minima: $(10,7)$ ✗, $(8,19)$ ✓, $(41,35)$ ✗, $(25,31)$ ✓, $(10,8)$ ✗, $(41,25)$ ✗, $(19,25)$ ✓ → 3.
pitfalls: Judging a merge by the original unsorted halves: the pair merge uses the sorted runs $[7,10]$ and $[8,19]$.
Missing the final merge: its halves are already split cleanly ($19 < 25$).
cse-2026-2-cs-22.verification: Independent check with maxima/minima of the original halves: final merge compares $\max\{10,7,8,19\} = 19$ with $\min\{41,35,25,31\} = 25$ → void; the right pair merge compares $\max\{41,35\} = 41$ with $\min\{25,31\} = 25$ → not void.

animation.title: Merge sort recursion (green = void merge, red = real interleaving)
animation.caption: Each internal node is one merge; its label is the merged output.

cse-2026-2-cs-23.approach: Count the 0-bits of the mask (host bits $h$); the block has $2^h$ addresses, of which the all-0s (network) and all-1s (broadcast) host parts cannot be assigned to interfaces.

steps.title: Count host bits
steps.body: Ones: $8 + 8 + 4 = 20$, so this is a /20 network (network + subnet part). Zeros: $32 - 20 = 12$ host bits.

steps.title: Usable addresses
steps.body:
Host part has $2^{12} = 4096$ patterns. Remove the all-0s pattern (network address) and the all-1s pattern (directed broadcast):

$$2^{12} - 2 = 4096 - 2 = 4094$$

cse-2026-2-cs-23.shortcut: Third octet $240 = 256 - 16$, so the block spans $16$ values of the third octet: $16 \times 256 = 4096$ addresses, minus 2 → $4094$.
pitfalls: Answering 4096 by forgetting the network and broadcast addresses.
Counting host bits as 4 (from 240 alone) and forgetting the fully-zero last octet.

cse-2026-2-cs-24.approach: Expand the hex word into its 32 bits, split as sign (1) | exponent (8) | fraction (23), and evaluate $(-1)^s \times 1.f \times 2^{e-127}$.
pitfalls: Forgetting the hidden leading 1 (gives $0.8828125 \times 32 = 28.25$).
Using bias 128 or forgetting the sign bit.
Splitting the hex digits as if each field were nibble-aligned — the exponent straddles the 1st and 3rd nibbles.

cse-2026-2-cs-25.approach: Scan each whitespace-separated chunk with longest match: an $id$ must start with a letter and may then absorb letters and digits, while a $number$ is a maximal run of digits. So a chunk splits only where a digit run is followed by a letter.

steps.title: How a chunk is cut
steps.body:
- Starting at a letter: $id$ takes every following letter **and** digit, so $x1$, $zz5$, $AaYcD$ are one token each.
- Starting at a digit: $number$ takes the digits; the first letter ends it and starts a new $id$. So $23mm \to 23,\ mm$.
- $ws$ separates chunks and is not counted.

steps.title: First five chunks
steps.body:
| chunk | tokens | count |
|---|---|---|
| x1 | id(x1) | 1 |
| 23mm | number(23), id(mm) | 2 |
| 78 | number(78) | 1 |
| y | id(y) | 1 |
| 7z | number(7), id(z) | 2 |

Running total: $1+2+1+1+2 = 7$.

steps.title: Last four chunks
steps.body:
| chunk | tokens | count |
|---|---|---|
| zz5 | id(zz5) | 1 |
| 14A | number(14), id(A) | 2 |
| 8H | number(8), id(H) | 2 |
| AaYcD | id(AaYcD) | 1 |

Subtotal $1+2+2+1 = 6$; total $7 + 6 = \mathbf{13}$.

cse-2026-2-cs-25.shortcut: $9$ chunks, plus one extra token for every chunk that starts with a digit and contains a letter ($23mm$, $7z$, $14A$, $8H$): $9 + 4 = 13$.
pitfalls: Splitting $x1$ or $zz5$ — an $id$ may contain digits after its first letter.
Treating $23mm$ as one token or as an error — longest match gives $number$ then $id$.
Counting whitespace as tokens.
cse-2026-2-cs-25.verification: By class: ids $x1, mm, y, z, zz5, A, H, AaYcD$ (8) and numbers $23, 78, 7, 14, 8$ (5); $8 + 5 = 13$.

cse-2026-2-cs-26.approach: The Jaccard coefficient is $\frac{|T_1 \cap T_2|}{|T_1 \cup T_2|} \ge 0$, with equality iff the two trees share no edge. So the question is whether $K_n$ ($n > 4$) has two **edge-disjoint** spanning trees — exhibit them.

steps.title: Lower bound 0
steps.body:
For edge sets $T_1, T_2$ the numerator $|T_1 \cap T_2| \ge 0$ and the denominator $|T_1 \cup T_2| \ge n - 1 > 0$, so $J \ge 0$, and $J = 0 \iff T_1 \cap T_2 = \varnothing$.

Edge count allows it: two disjoint trees need $2(n-1)$ edges, and $\binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} \ge 2(n-1) \iff n \ge 4$.

steps.title: Build two disjoint trees
steps.body:
Label the vertices $v_1, \dots, v_n$.

- $T_1 = \{v_1v_3, v_1v_4, \dots, v_1v_n\} \cup \{v_2v_3\}$: a star at $v_1$ on $v_3..v_n$, with $v_2$ hung on $v_3$. Edges: $(n-2) + 1 = n-1$, connected ⇒ spanning tree.
- $T_2 = \{v_2v_1, v_2v_4, \dots, v_2v_n\} \cup \{v_3v_4\}$: a star at $v_2$ on $v_1, v_4..v_n$, with $v_3$ hung on $v_4$. Edges: $1 + (n-3) + 1 = n-1$, connected ⇒ spanning tree.

No edge is shared ($v_1v_2$, $v_3v_4$ and $v_2v_k$ are not in $T_1$).

steps.title: Compute J
steps.body:
$$J(T_1, T_2) = \frac{|T_1 \cap T_2|}{|T_1 \cup T_2|} = \frac{0}{2(n-1)} = 0$$
Since $J \ge 0$ always, the lowest possible value is $\mathbf{0}$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $\frac1n$ does not even arise naturally: one shared edge gives $\frac{1}{2n-3}$, and edge-disjoint trees give $0$, which is smaller.
$\frac{1}{2n-3}$ is the value when the trees share exactly **one** edge ($|\cap| = 1$, $|\cup| = 2(n-1) - 1$); it is not the minimum because sharing no edge is possible.
$K_n$ with $n > 4$ has two edge-disjoint spanning trees, so the intersection can be empty and $J = 0$.
$\frac{1}{n-1}$ would be $|\cap| = 1$ over a union of only $n-1$ edges — impossible for two different trees, and anyway larger than $0$.

cse-2026-2-cs-26.shortcut: Nash-Williams/Tutte: $K_n$ contains $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ edge-disjoint spanning trees, which is $\ge 2$ for $n \ge 4$. Disjoint ⇒ $J = 0$.
pitfalls: Assuming every two spanning trees must share an edge.
Computing the Jaccard value for trees sharing one edge ($\frac{1}{2n-3}$) and stopping there.
cse-2026-2-cs-26.verification: In $K_5$: $T_1 = \{13, 14, 15, 23\}$ and $T_2 = \{12, 24, 25, 34\}$ each have 4 edges, reach all 5 vertices, and share nothing; $J = 0/8 = 0$.

animation.title: K₅ with two edge-disjoint spanning trees

cse-2026-2-cs-27.approach: In a DAG, relax edges in topological order: one topological sort plus one relaxation per edge gives all shortest-path lengths in $\Theta(m + n)$, works even with negative weights, and no algorithm can avoid reading the edges.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body:
1. Topologically sort $G$ (DFS finishing times or Kahn's algorithm): $\Theta(m + n)$.
2. Set $d[s] = 0$, $d[v] = \infty$ otherwise.
3. For each vertex $u$ in topological order, for each edge $(u, v)$: $d[v] = \min(d[v],\, d[u] + w(u, v))$.

steps.title: Why it is correct
steps.body: Every path into $v$ uses only vertices that come before $v$ in topological order. When $u$ is processed, all of its predecessors were already processed, so $d[u]$ is final; relaxing $u$'s out-edges therefore propagates exact distances (induction along the order). Negative weights are fine — a DAG has no cycles at all.

steps.title: Running time and lower bound
steps.body:
Sorting: $\Theta(m + n)$. Relaxation: each vertex once and each edge once, $\Theta(n + m)$. Total $\Theta(m + n)$.

It cannot be beaten in the worst case: any edge that is not read could be the one that shortens a path, so $\Omega(m)$ edge inspections (and $\Omega(n)$ outputs) are needed.

optionAnalysis.reason: Topological sort + one relaxation per edge; linear and optimal.
Dijkstra with a Fibonacci heap — slower than necessary, and it is not even correct if some weights are negative, which a weighted DAG allows.
Bellman–Ford's $\Theta(nm)$ handles general graphs; on a DAG a single pass in topological order already suffices.
$\Theta(n^3)$ is Floyd–Warshall (all pairs) — far more than a single source needs.

cse-2026-2-cs-27.shortcut: DAG + single source ⇒ “topo-sort then relax” ⇒ linear time. Remember it as the DAG-SP algorithm from CLRS §24.2.
pitfalls: Reaching for Dijkstra by habit; it is neither the fastest here nor safe with negative weights.
Choosing Bellman–Ford because weights may be negative — the acyclicity removes the need for $n-1$ passes.
cse-2026-2-cs-27.verification: Sanity check of optimality: the input itself has size $\Theta(m + n)$, so a $\Theta(m + n)$ algorithm is the best possible order of growth.

cse-2026-2-cs-28.approach: Let $d_k = A[k+1] - A[k]$. The condition says $d_i > d_j$ whenever $i > j$, i.e. the difference sequence is strictly increasing — which is equivalent to checking only **adjacent** pairs $d_{k+1} > d_k$. One linear scan does it, and every element must be read.

steps.title: Rewrite the condition
steps.body:
With $d_k = A[k+1] - A[k]$ for $k = 1, \dots, n-1$, the condition is
$$\forall\, i > j:\ d_i > d_j \iff d_1 < d_2 < \dots < d_{n-1}.$$
Checking $d_{k+1} > d_k$ for $k = 1, \dots, n-2$ suffices: by transitivity $d_j < d_{j+1} < \dots < d_i$ for any $i > j$.

steps.title: Linear algorithm
steps.body: Scan $k = 1$ to $n-2$, compute $d_k$ and $d_{k+1}$, and reject as soon as $d_{k+1} \le d_k$; accept at the end. That is $n - 2$ comparisons and $O(n)$ time.

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: Any correct algorithm must read every $A[k]$ in the worst case. Take a valid array such as $A[k] = k^2$ (differences $3, 5, 7, \dots$). If some $A[k]$ is never read, changing it by a large enough amount changes $d_{k-1}$ and $d_k$ in opposite directions and breaks the strict increase — but the algorithm would give the same answer. So $\Omega(n)$, and the worst case is $\Theta(n)$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Adjacent-difference scan is $O(n)$, and the adversary argument gives $\Omega(n)$.
$\Theta(\log n)$ would mean reading only a few elements; any unread element can break the property, so this is impossible.
Sorting the differences is unnecessary — their order must already be the index order, which a scan checks.
$\Theta(n^2)$ is the literal check over all pairs $(i, j)$; transitivity reduces it to adjacent pairs.

cse-2026-2-cs-28.shortcut: “For all $i > j$, $f(i) > f(j)$” = “$f$ strictly increasing” = check neighbours only ⇒ one pass ⇒ $\Theta(n)$.
pitfalls: Implementing the quantifier literally with two nested loops.
Thinking binary search applies because the differences are “sorted” — that is what has to be verified, not assumed.
cse-2026-2-cs-28.verification: Example $A = [1, 2, 4, 7, 11]$: $d = 1, 2, 3, 4$ (increasing) ✓. Change $A[3]$ from $4$ to $10$: $d = 1, 8, -3, 4$ — the scan rejects at $k = 2$ ($-3 \le 8$).

cse-2026-2-cs-29.approach: $T[i][j]$ depends on its **upper** neighbour $T[i-1][j]$ and **left** neighbour $T[i][j-1]$. An evaluation order is correct iff both are final before $T[i][j]$ is written. Check that for row-major order (B1) and anti-diagonal order (B2).

steps.title: Dependencies
steps.body:
Row 0 and column 0 are base cases with value 1, and both algorithms start with every entry equal to 1, so the boundary is already correct and is never overwritten (both loops start at $1$).

For $1 \le i, j \le n$: $T[i][j]$ needs $T[i-1][j]$ (one row up) and $T[i][j-1]$ (one column left). Each is a boundary cell or an interior cell with smaller $i + j$.

steps.title: B1: row by row
steps.body:
When B1 computes $T[i][j]$:

- $T[i-1][j]$: row $i-1$ was finished in the previous iteration of the outer loop (or is row 0).
- $T[i][j-1]$: computed just before in the same row (or is column 0).

Both are final, so each entry is computed once with correct inputs. **B1 is correct.** (For $n = 3$: $T[1][\cdot] = 5, 17, 53$; $T[2][\cdot] = 13, 73, 325$; $T[3][\cdot] = 29, 233, 1349$.)

scene.caption: Row-major order: each row uses the finished row above

steps.title: B2: anti-diagonal by anti-diagonal
steps.body:
In pass $s$ B2 writes exactly the interior cells with $i + j = s$ (the $If$ filters the $n^2$ pairs). Their inputs $T[i-1][j]$ and $T[i][j-1]$ have index sum $s - 1$: either boundary cells, or interior cells written in pass $s-1$. By induction on $s$, every pass reads only final values.

Every interior cell has $2 \le i + j \le 2n$, so each is written in exactly one pass. **B2 is correct** too (it just wastes time: $\Theta(n^3)$ iterations).

scene.caption: Pass s = 4 writes (1,3), (2,2), (3,1) from the finished diagonal s = 3

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Both algorithms respect the dependency order (each is a topological order of the DAG “up-neighbour, left-neighbour → cell”), so both compute the correct table: option **(A)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Row-major order and anti-diagonal order both compute every cell after its up and left neighbours.
Assumes the anti-diagonal sweep reads unfinished cells; but the inputs of a cell on diagonal $s$ lie on diagonal $s - 1$, finished in the previous pass.
Assumes row-major order is wrong; the up-neighbour is in the finished previous row and the left-neighbour was just computed.
Confuses inefficiency ($B_2$ loops $\Theta(n^3)$ times) with incorrectness; neither algorithm ever uses a stale value.

cse-2026-2-cs-29.shortcut: Any order in which $(i-1, j)$ and $(i, j-1)$ come before $(i, j)$ works. Row-major: yes. Increasing $i + j$: yes (both neighbours have sum $i + j - 1$). ⇒ both correct.
pitfalls: Thinking the initial 1s are a bug — they are exactly the base cases for row 0 and column 0.
Equating “slow” with “incorrect” for B2.
